opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and some of them are more about convenience than about anything deep.

The first and most obvious one is that code and math are domains where the reward is relatively easy to define. In math you have a final answer you can check. In code you have unit tests, you can run the program, and it either passes or it doesn't. Reinforcement learning has always needed a reward signal, and for a long time the bottleneck was that in most real-world tasks the reward is fuzzy, expensive, or requires a human to judge. Code and math are the places where you get a fairly clean, automatic, scalable signal. So it's natural that people went there first. It's like looking for your keys under the streetlight, partly because that's where the light is.

The second reason is that these domains feel like they test reasoning in a fairly pure way. There's an intuition, and I think it's partly right, that if a model learns to do multi-step reasoning in math, to break a problem down, try something, notice it's wrong, backtrack, that kind of skill might transfer. And we did see some of that. Training on math and code with RL seemed to improve the model's general thinking behavior, its ability to produce longer and more careful chains of thought. So people got excited that these are almost like a gym for general reasoning.

The third reason is more about the research community. Benchmarks drive attention. Math competitions, coding contests, SWE-bench: they're concrete, they're legible, everyone understands what a high score means. It's very easy to write a paper or make an announcement around them. So there's a self-reinforcing loop where the measurable domains get the effort.

But I'd push back a bit on the idea that this is the whole story. I've been thinking a lot about what I'd call the "second half" of AI. In the first half, the game was: build better methods, better models, and hill-climb on benchmarks. Now we have a recipe that kind of works: large-scale pretraining, plus reasoning, plus RL. It generalizes surprisingly well to these benchmark-style tasks. The more important question becomes: what are the tasks that actually matter, and how do we evaluate them? Real-world utility is not a math competition. A lot of valuable work is long-horizon, involves interacting with people, has ambiguous goals, and has no clean verifier.

So I think code and math got so much attention because they are where RL was easiest to make work, and they gave us strong evidence that the recipe is real. Code is also special in another way: it's not just a task, it's an affordance. It's how an agent acts on the digital world. So progress in code has a kind of leverage that pure math may not. But the frontier now is figuring out how to bring that same kind of learning signal into messier, more human domains. That's less about the algorithm and more about defining the right environments and the right evaluations.

r001.rationale: The response says code and math were studied early because rewards were easy to define and benchmarks were legible; it does not attribute their prominence to simply having been studied first.

r002.rationale: It identifies clean, automatic, scalable reward signals—such as checking math answers and running code tests—as a reason these domains were natural early choices for RL.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify avoiding the need for an environment as a reason for choosing code and math.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest answer is that code and math are the two places where you can get a cheap, reliable reward signal at scale. If you want to do reinforcement learning, the thing you actually need is not just a task, it's a verifier. In math you have a final answer you can check, and in code you have unit tests or a compiler that tells you whether the thing runs. That's a very clean reward. You don't need a human to grade every sample, and you don't need a learned reward model that can be hacked. So from an engineering perspective they're the natural first targets.

The second reason is that they're hard in the right way. A lot of earlier RL work was on games, and games are nice because they also have clear rewards, but they don't transfer much to the real world. Math and code sit in this interesting middle ground: they're well-defined enough that you can verify them, but the reasoning required is general enough that it seems to carry over. When a model learns to plan, decompose a problem, check its own work, and recover from a mistake while solving a competition math problem, those are the same behaviors you want in any agentic setting. So people hoped, and I think the evidence increasingly shows, that you're not just teaching math, you're teaching reasoning.

And there's a practical point too. The researchers building these systems are themselves programmers and mathematicians, so they have good intuitions about the tasks, the benchmarks already exist, and there's a huge amount of pretraining data in these domains. The model already has the prior knowledge. RL is mostly about eliciting and sharpening behaviors the model can almost do, rather than teaching it from scratch, so starting where the prior is strong makes sense.

But I'd also say we shouldn't over-index on them. The reason RL works there is the verifier, and most of the world doesn't come with a verifier. If you want an agent that does your taxes, browses the web, or writes a research paper, the reward is fuzzy and delayed, and the environment is messy. So I see math and code as the proof of concept. The real question for the next few years is whether we can build environments and evaluation methods for all the tasks that aren't so clean, and I think that's actually where most of the interesting work is now.

r001.rationale: The response calls math and code natural first targets because they have strong priors, existing benchmarks, and verifiable rewards; it does not say they were prominent because they were studied first.

r002.rationale: It explicitly identifies cheap, reliable reward signals from mathematical answer checks and code tests or compilers as a reason these domains are natural early targets.

r003.rationale: The response emphasizes verifiers and says other tasks need environments and evaluation methods, but does not identify not needing an environment as a reason for choosing math and code.

astra-6.text:
I think a big reason is that code and mathematics give us a relatively clear reward signal. In math, you can often check whether the final answer is correct. In coding, you can run the program and see whether it passes tests. So you can let a model try different approaches and learn from the results without having a person judge every attempt.

But verifiability alone isn’t enough. These domains also contain a huge range of problems, from very simple to very difficult, and solving them involves reusable skills: breaking a problem into smaller pieces, choosing an approach, checking intermediate results, and recovering from mistakes. That creates an opportunity for reinforcement learning to improve something more general than the answer to one particular question.

I would still distinguish generalizing to new math or coding problems from generalizing to entirely different activities. If a model improves on an unseen math benchmark, that’s meaningful, but it doesn’t automatically mean it will become better at doing research or making decisions in the real world. Those settings often have ambiguous goals and delayed feedback.

So I think the attention comes partly from their importance, but also from how tractable they are experimentally. We have a way to train, a way to measure progress, and a reasonable hypothesis that some of the skills being learned will transfer. How far that transfer goes is the more interesting question.

r001.rationale: The response says these domains are important and experimentally tractable, but does not say they were prominent because they were studied first.

r002.rationale: It identifies clear, checkable rewards: math answers can be verified and code can be run against tests.

r003.rationale: It describes checking math answers and running code, but does not identify avoiding the need for an environment as a reason for choosing these domains.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big reason is that code and mathematics give us a very convenient way to verify an answer. In math, you can often check whether the final answer is correct. In code, you can run the program and see whether it passes the tests. So you can let the model try different approaches and give it a reward without needing a human to judge every attempt.

And these are domains where spending more time thinking can actually help. You can break a problem into steps, try something, notice a mistake, and revise. Reinforcement learning can potentially encourage those behaviors, rather than just teaching the model to imitate an existing solution.

But I would distinguish getting better on new problems within a domain from generalizing to entirely different domains. If you train on math and improve on unseen math problems, that is meaningful, but it doesn’t automatically mean you’ve learned a general reasoning ability that transfers everywhere. Code and math get a lot of attention partly because progress is easier to train and measure there. The more interesting question is which parts of that progress carry over to tasks where success is harder to verify.

r001.rationale: The response says code and math are easier to train and measure, but does not say they were studied first.

r002.rationale: It explains that answers in math can be checked and code can be run against tests, allowing rewards without human judgment.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify the absence of a need for an environment as a reason these domains were chosen.
